name: Hierarchical Data Structures
text:
# Hierarchical Data Structures


## Overview
Hierarchical Data Structures are spatial [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures that organize volume data into a tree or pyramid to accelerate ray traversal by skipping empty or uniform regions. They solve the problem of inefficiently sampling large, sparse voxel datasets by allowing rays to bypass large volumes of background data in logarithmic time relative to the dataset size [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial]. Unlike flat [grid traversal](#14347-grid-traversal-one-pass-over-allocated.md) which samples every voxel along the ray, these methods use the hierarchy to determine occupancy, switching to fine-grained sampling only when occupied leaves are reached [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent [G]. The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial][G].

1.  **Child Selection:** For a node with center $\mathbf{c}$ and half-extent $s$, the ray position $\mathbf{p}$ determines the child index $k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}$:
    $$
    k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(p_x \ge c_x) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(p_y \ge c_y) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(p_z \ge c_z)
    $$
    where $\mathbb{I}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial][G].

2.  **[Empty Space Skipping](#1002-empty-space-skipping.md):** If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree [G]. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter $t$ to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node [S1, unofficial][G].

3.  **Leaf Handling:** Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data [S1, unofficial][G].

4.  **Backtracking:** Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch [G]. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU) [G].

## Subtopics

### [Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization](1663-hierarchical-spatial-enumeration-optimization.md)
A method encoding spatial coherence into a [pyramid of binary volumes](#1663-hierarchical-spatial-enumeration-optimization.md). It solves the problem of inefficiently traversing large voxel datasets by allowing rays to skip large empty regions in logarithmic time relative to ray length. Unlike geometric ray tracing which uses bounding volumes or condensed [octree representations](#2340-sparse-voxel-octree-representation.md), this method uses a complete [octree structure](#2792-octree-based-structures.md) (pyramid of binary volumes) specifically optimized for the spatially ordered, single-sample nature of volume data.

### [Jiang et al. Acceleration Structure](1673-jiang-et-al-acceleration-structure.md)
A hierarchical data structure designed to efficiently locate active cells within a scalar volume for both direct and indirect visualization approaches. It solves the problem of redundant [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) through inactive background regions by identifying and rendering only the relevant active cells. Unlike pure image-order methods, it is classified as a hybrid object-order and [image-order approach](#2938-image-order-rendering-loop.md), meaning its performance and structure are dependent on the rendering resolution.

### [Silhouette Image Space Acceleration Structure (Mip Pyramid)](3731-silhouette-image-space-acceleration-structure-mip-pyramid.md)
This method accelerates [voxelization](#12-voxelization.md) culling decisions by providing conservative bounds on silhouette coverage for 3D voxels. It solves the problem of efficiently determining whether a voxel intersects with the visual hull defined by multiple camera views without performing expensive per-pixel ray casting. It is distinguished from sibling methods by operating in image space using a mip-pyramid hierarchy over pre-filtered silhouette masks, inspired by hierarchical z-buffering, to guarantee no small features are missed or holes created in the resulting voxel grid.

### [Flex-block tree](9716-flex-block-tree.md)
A hierarchical data structure derived from a kd-tree, designed to distribute massive volume data across [distributed rendering](#15077-system-level-primitive-sharding.md) nodes while ensuring [load balancing](#19162-load-balancing.md) and deterministic view-dependent ordering. It solves the problem of efficient data distribution and ray-task scheduling in distributed ray casting and ray tracing by partitioning space into "flex-blocks" that tightly crop empty space. Unlike traditional space subdivision methods that alternate axis cuts, the [flex-block partition](#9716-flex-block-tree.md) allows flexible cut orientations to accommodate scenes with disproportionate dimensions, and it provides a dependency graph for image composition in ray casting and [traversal acceleration](#10779-traversal-acceleration.md) in ray tracing.

### [Data Structure and Indexing](12420-data-structure-and-indexing.md)
Defines the memory layout and access mechanisms for hierarchical volume representations, enabling efficient ray traversal by mapping spatial relationships to linear or texture-based addresses. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on the low-level encoding of node connectivity (such as neighbor pointers or binary tree arrays) rather than high-level traversal heuristics or specific [compression](#4-compression.md) algorithms.

### [Spatial Hierarchies](13154-spatial-hierarchies.md)
Accelerate volume rendering by performing point location through recursive search through the [tree structure](#4139-tree-based-structures-octree-pointer-tree-sparse-voxel-dag.md). They organize spatial data into a hierarchy of bounding volumes, allowing the renderer to quickly cull empty or irrelevant regions. What sets them apart from sibling methods like Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization is their explicit geometric subdivision of space rather than linear enumeration or silhouette-based approximations.

### [Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition](13647-brick-of-bricks-decomposition.md)
A storage format for volume data where the volume is stored as a [flat hierarchy of bricks](#13647-brick-of-bricks-decomposition.md) of size $n^3$ to improve cache-coherence in volume traversal. It arises from not fully expanding an octree into single-voxel leaf nodes. It sets itself apart from fully expanded octrees by maintaining a hierarchical structure of larger blocks rather than individual voxels, and from flat grids by providing spatial locality through block-based indexing.

### Spatial Partitioning Tree for Unstructured Data
- [S1, unofficial] A preprocessing step that performs a parallel, synchronized partitioning of the volume data to produce a hierarchical spatial tree. This tree is used during rendering to optimize the [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) process, reduce runtime memory consumption, and speed up cell searching for zoom-in viewing.
- [S1, unofficial] Perform parallel, synchronized partitioning of the volume data.
- [S1, unofficial] Construct a hierarchical representation (spatial tree) of the data space.
- [S1, unofficial] Use the spatial tree during rendering to guide the compositing process.
- [S1, unofficial] Use the spatial tree to reduce runtime memory consumption.
- [S1, unofficial] Use the spatial tree to speed up cell searching for zoom-in viewing operations.

### HiGS
- [S2, unofficial] A hierarchical rendering architecture that achieves real-time performance through adaptive level selection and efficient GPU execution.

### Cell-tree Peeling
- [S3, unofficial] An efficient cell-processing schedule for the next frame determined using a ray dependency graph (the cell-tree). When a render-node becomes available, the cell with the longest queue is assigned to it.
- [S3, unofficial] The cell-tree represents ray dependencies between cells. Each node in the cell-tree has an associated cell ID, and more than one node may have the same cell ID.
- [S3, unofficial] The algorithm exploits frame-to-frame coherence by using the cell tree to find potential cache savings links. A schedule with any combination of non-conflicting link groups is a feasible one, and the optimal schedule for a single render-node includes a maximal group of cache savings links.
- [S3, unofficial] As long as a cell of data is in local memory, all rays on the corresponding queue are processed before it is replaced with another cell.
- [S3, unofficial] The tree is processed starting with the leaves by peeling the tree nodes with the same cell ID and adding it to the reverse schedule.
- [S3, unofficial] An interim tree is maintained by keeping a list of nodes that have not been included in the schedule.
- [S3, unofficial] Cache savings links are found by [gathering](#9569-gathering.md) leaf nodes which correspond to the same cell.
- [S3, unofficial] The cell-tree peeling algorithm performs well and has polynomial worst time.

## Background
The concept of hierarchical spatial partitioning for volume rendering originated in the context of parallel and distributed rendering systems. Early work focused on distributing unstructured data across processors to balance load and reduce memory consumption [S1, unofficial]. The use of spatial trees to accelerate cell searching and compositing was introduced to handle large-scale datasets where naive traversal was too slow [S1, unofficial]. More recent developments include hierarchical architectures for real-time rendering, such as HiGS, which leverage adaptive level selection [S2, unofficial], and specialized structures like the flex-block tree for distributed ray tracing [S3, unofficial].
